course.title: JavaScript: From Beginner to Advanced
course.description: Master JavaScript fundamentals, DOM manipulation, events, APIs and modern JavaScript.

lessons.title: Variables, Types & Operators
lessons.body:
Variables, Types & Operators

Variables store values you reuse later. Declare them with let (reassignable), const (cannot be reassigned) or the old var (avoid it — it leaks out of blocks). JavaScript figures out the type for you: "hello" is a string, 42 is a number, true is a boolean, undefined means declared but never given a value, and null means deliberately empty.

Operators do the work: + - * / % for maths, === for strict comparison (always prefer it over ==, which converts types first — "5" == 5 is true but "5" === 5 is false), and && / || for combining conditions. Watch out for + with a string: 5 + "5" gives "55" because the number is converted to a string first.

let score = 10;
const passMark = 40;
score = score + 5;
console.log(typeof score);   // "number"
console.log(score === 15);   // true
console.log("Total: " + score); // "Total: 15"

Step by step: score starts at 10, then score + 5 makes it 15. typeof tells you a value's type, and === checks value and type together.

  • Key points
  • Use const by default, let when the value must change, never var.
  • === compares value and type; == converts types and surprises you.
  • + with a string concatenates instead of adding.

mcqs.q: Which keyword declares a variable that cannot be reassigned?
mcqs.why: const creates a binding that cannot be reassigned; let allows reassignment and var is the old function-scoped declaration.

mcqs.q: What is the result of typeof "42"?
mcqs.why: typeof reports the value's type, and "42" in quotes is a string, so typeof returns "string".

mcqs.q: What does 5 + "5" evaluate to?
mcqs.why: When + meets a string it concatenates: the number 5 is converted to "5" and joined, giving the string "55".

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT a primitive type in JavaScript?
mcqs.why: string, number and boolean are primitives; object is a reference type (arrays and functions are objects too).

mcqs.q: What does this print? let x; console.log(x);
mcqs.why: A declared variable with no assignment holds the value undefined — it exists, it just has no value yet.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.answer: Multiplication runs before subtraction, so discount * 2 is 20, and 50 - 20 is 30.

lessons.title: Functions & Scope
lessons.body:
Functions & Scope

A function packages reusable behaviour: you define it once with function and call it as often as you like. Values listed in the definition are parameters; the values you pass when calling are arguments. A function without a return statement returns undefined. Arrow functions (const add = (a, b) => a + b;) are a shorter way to write small functions.

Scope decides where a variable can be seen. A variable declared inside a function is visible only there; let and const are also block-scoped, so they disappear outside the { } they were declared in, while var ignores blocks. Function declarations are hoisted — you can call them before their definition in the file — but const arrow functions are not, so calling one early throws a ReferenceError.

function greet(name) {
  return "Hello, " + name + "!";
}
const square = (n) => n * n;
console.log(greet("Sid")); // "Hello, Sid!"
console.log(square(4));    // 16

Step by step: greet takes the argument "Sid", plugs it into the parameter name, and returns the finished string. square does the same job as an arrow function in one line.

  • Key points
  • Parameters are placeholders in the definition; arguments are the real values passed at the call.
  • No return means the function returns undefined.
  • let/const are block-scoped; var is not.
  • Function declarations hoist; const arrow functions do not.

mcqs.q: What does a function return when it has no return statement?
mcqs.why: JavaScript functions return undefined by default when execution reaches the end without hitting return.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct arrow-function syntax for adding two numbers?
mcqs.why: An arrow function assigns a function value to a variable: parameters in parentheses, then =>, then the expression to return.

mcqs.q: Which declaration is block-scoped, so it cannot be used outside its { } block?
mcqs.why: let (and const) are scoped to the block they are declared in; var is scoped to the enclosing function instead.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
options: A parameter is the placeholder in the definition; an argument is the value passed at the call
A parameter is the value passed; an argument is the placeholder
Parameters only exist in arrow functions
mcqs.why: The parameter is the named slot in the function definition; the argument is the actual value supplied when the function is called.

mcqs.q: What happens when you call a const arrow function before its definition line runs?
options: It works, because all functions hoist
ReferenceError — it is in the temporal dead zone
mcqs.why: Only function declarations hoist fully. A const arrow function cannot be used before its line executes — that is the temporal dead zone.

tasks.title: Trace the variables
tasks.prompt: Work out the value of x step by step, then say what is printed.
tasks.answer: double(4) returns 8, so x is 8; x + 1 is 9, which is what console.log prints.
tasks.hint: Follow the call first: what does double(4) return?

lessons.title: Arrays & Objects in Depth
lessons.body:
Arrays & Objects in Depth

Arrays hold ordered lists and objects hold named values. Arrays come with methods: push adds to the end, pop removes from the end, map builds a new array by transforming each item, and filter keeps only the items that pass a test. Crucially, map returns a new array while forEach returns undefined — use map when you want a result.

Objects group related data: const user = { name: "Sid", age: 19 }. Read properties with dot notation (user.name) or bracket notation (user["name"]) — brackets are required when the key is stored in a variable. Destructuring pulls values out in one line: const { name, age } = user;. JSON.stringify turns an object into a JSON string for storage or sending to a server.

const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];
const doubled = nums.map(n => n * 2);
const evens = nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0);
console.log(doubled); // [2, 4, 6, 8]
console.log(evens);   // [2, 4]

Step by step: map runs n * 2 on every element and collects the results into a new array; the original nums is unchanged. filter keeps only numbers where n % 2 === 0.

  • Key points
  • map returns a new array; forEach returns undefined.
  • Use bracket notation when the property name is in a variable.
  • Destructuring extracts several properties in one line.
  • JSON.stringify converts an object to a JSON string.

mcqs.q: What is the length of this array afterwards? const a = [1, 2, 3]; a.push(4);
mcqs.why: push adds one element to the end, so [1, 2, 3] becomes [1, 2, 3, 4], which has length 4.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between map and forEach?
options: map returns a new array; forEach returns undefined
forEach returns a new array; map returns undefined
mcqs.why: map builds and returns a new array from the callback's return values; forEach just runs the callback for side effects and returns undefined.

mcqs.q: How do you read an object property when the key is stored in a variable called key?
mcqs.why: Dot notation looks for a literal property named 'key'; bracket notation evaluates the variable, so obj[key] reads the property whose name the variable holds.

mcqs.q: What does JSON.stringify({a: 1}) return?
mcqs.why: JSON.stringify serialises a value to a JSON string, so the object becomes the string '{"a":1}'.

mcqs.q: Which array method removes the LAST element?
mcqs.why: pop removes and returns the last element; shift removes the first, slice copies a portion, and splice(0, 1) removes the first.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.answer: map doubles every element, so doubled is [2, 4, 6, 8]; index 1 is the second element, 4.
tasks.hint: Work out the whole doubled array first, then pick index 1.

lessons.title: Async JavaScript & Fetch API
lessons.body:
Async JavaScript & Fetch API

JavaScript runs one thing at a time, so slow work like network requests is asynchronous: you start it and get the result later instead of freezing the page. A Promise represents a value that will arrive in the future. fetch(url) returns a promise that resolves to the response; response.json() returns another promise that resolves to the parsed data. async/await lets you write this in straight-line style: await pauses the function until the promise settles.

Errors need handling: .catch() catches a rejected promise, and try/catch does the same around await. Remember that fetch only rejects on network failure — a 404 still resolves, so check response.ok yourself. And setTimeout never runs early: its callback waits until the current synchronous code finishes, even with a 0 ms delay.

async function getUser(id) {
  const res = await fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/" + id);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("User not found");
  const user = await res.json();
  return user.name;
}
getUser(1).then(name => console.log(name));

Step by step: fetch starts the request and await pauses getUser until the response arrives. res.ok guards against HTTP errors, then await res.json() parses the body and the name is returned.

  • Key points
  • fetch() returns a Promise; await pauses until it settles.
  • response.json() also returns a Promise.
  • Check response.ok — fetch does not reject on HTTP errors like 404.
  • setTimeout callbacks run only after the current synchronous code finishes.

mcqs.q: What does fetch() return?
options: A Promise that resolves to the response
mcqs.why: fetch starts the request and immediately returns a Promise; the response arrives later when the promise resolves.

mcqs.q: Where can await be used?
mcqs.why: await is only valid inside a function declared with async (top-level await in modules aside, plain scripts require async functions).

mcqs.q: What does .catch() do on a promise?
options: It runs when the promise resolves
It converts the result to JSON
mcqs.why: .catch registers a handler that runs if the promise rejects, so errors can be dealt with instead of crashing.

mcqs.q: What does response.json() return?
options: A Promise resolving to the parsed JSON
mcqs.why: Parsing the body is itself asynchronous, so response.json() returns a promise that resolves to the parsed data.

mcqs.q: What is the output order of: console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0); console.log("C");
mcqs.why: setTimeout schedules its callback after the current synchronous code finishes, so A and C print first, then B — even with a 0 ms delay.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.answer: A prints first, then C — the setTimeout callback is queued and only runs after the synchronous code finishes, so B prints last.
tasks.hint: setTimeout never interrupts code that is already running.

lessons.title: ES6+ Modern Features
lessons.body:
ES6+ Modern Features

Modern JavaScript (ES6 and later) added shortcuts that make code shorter and safer. Template literals use backticks and ${ } to embed values: `Hello ${name}`. Destructuring unpacks objects and arrays: const { name } = user; and const [first] = list;. The spread operator ... copies or merges arrays and objects: [...a, ...b] and {...defaults, ...overrides}.

Other essentials: default parameters (function greet(name = "Guest")), rest parameters (function sum(...nums) collects extra arguments into an array), and optional chaining (user?.address?.city) which returns undefined instead of throwing when something in the chain is null or undefined. Modules split code across files with export and import.

const user = { name: "Sid", age: 19 };
const { name, age } = user;
const more = { ...user, city: "Warangal" };
console.log(`Hello ${name}, age ${age}`); // "Hello Sid, age 19"
console.log(more.city); // "Warangal"

Step by step: destructuring copies name and age out of user; the spread copies all of user into more and adds city; the template literal fills in the values.

  • Key points
  • Template literals use backticks and ${ }.
  • Destructuring unpacks values; spread ... copies or merges.
  • Default parameters supply a value when no argument is passed.
  • Optional chaining ?. returns undefined instead of throwing.

mcqs.q: Which characters delimit a template literal?
mcqs.why: Template literals are wrapped in backticks, which is what allows ${ } placeholders inside the string.

mcqs.q: What does the spread operator do in [...a, ...b]?
options: It creates a new array with all elements of a followed by all of b
mcqs.why: Spread expands each array in place, so the result is one new array containing a's elements then b's elements.

mcqs.q: What does const { name } = user; do?
options: It extracts the name property into a variable called name
mcqs.why: Object destructuring pulls the named property out of the object into a variable of the same name.

mcqs.q: What happens when you call greet() if it is defined as function greet(name = "Guest")?
mcqs.why: A default parameter supplies its value whenever the argument is missing (or explicitly undefined).

mcqs.q: What does user?.address?.city return when user.address is undefined?
mcqs.why: Optional chaining short-circuits: when address is null or undefined it stops and returns undefined instead of throwing.

tasks.prompt: Fill in the missing code so the program prints the user's name.
tasks.answer: Destructuring pulls the name property out of user into a variable called name, so console.log(name) prints Sid.

lessons.title: Mini Project: Weather App
lessons.body:
Mini Project: Weather App

Time to put it all together: a weather app that takes a city name, fetches live weather, and shows it on the page. The flow is: read the city from an input, build the API URL, fetch it with await, check response.ok (a mistyped city returns 404, and fetch will not reject on its own), parse the JSON, and render the temperature and description into the page. Show a "Loading..." message before the request and an error message if anything fails.

Structure the code in small functions: getWeather(city) does the fetching and returns data, showWeather(data) updates the page, and a click handler wires the button to both. Keep the API key in one clearly-marked constant at the top (in a real shipped app a key belongs on a server, not in client code — here a free demo key or placeholder keeps the project runnable).

const API_KEY = "YOUR_API_KEY"; // replace with a free key
async function getWeather(city) {
  const url = "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=" + city + "&units=metric&appid=" + API_KEY;
  const res = await fetch(url);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("City not found");
  return res.json();
}

Step by step: the city goes into the URL, fetch calls the API, res.ok catches bad cities, and res.json() gives the weather data your display function can render.

  • Key points
  • Read input, fetch, check response.ok, parse, render — in that order.
  • Show a loading state before the request and an error state on failure.
  • Split the work into small functions: fetch, render, wire-up.
  • API keys belong on a server in real apps, not in shipped client code.

mcqs.q: What is the first step in the weather app's flow?
options: Read the city name from the input
mcqs.why: Everything starts with the user's city — you cannot build the API URL until you have read it from the input.

mcqs.q: Why must you check response.ok after fetching the weather?
options: fetch only rejects on network failure, not on HTTP errors like 404
response.ok is required for JSON parsing
mcqs.why: A mistyped city returns HTTP 404, but fetch still resolves — only a network failure rejects — so you must check res.ok yourself.

mcqs.q: Where should a real API key live in a production app?
options: On the server, never shipped in client code
mcqs.why: A key in client-side JavaScript is visible to anyone who opens the page, so production keys are kept server-side and the browser calls your server.

mcqs.q: Which method converts a fetch response into usable data?
mcqs.why: response.json() parses the body as JSON and returns a promise of the resulting object.

mcqs.q: What is the best way to show the user that weather is loading?
options: Do nothing until the data arrives
Set a "Loading..." message before the await, then replace it afterwards
mcqs.why: Updating the page before the await gives instant feedback; the result replaces the message once the promise resolves.

tasks.title: Build the weather app
tasks.prompt: Build a weather app: an input and a button, fetch the weather for the typed city, and show the temperature, weather description and city name. Handle a mistyped city with a friendly error message and show "Loading..." while fetching.
tasks.expected: Working app: typing a city and clicking the button shows its temperature and description; a wrong city shows an error; "Loading..." appears while fetching
tasks.answer: Split it into three small functions — getWeather(city) for the fetch, showWeather(data) for rendering, and a click handler that ties them together. Test with a real city first, then a fake one.
tasks.hint: Start with the HTML input and button, then the fetch.
